category: Partitive nouns — how to count the uncountable

entries.meaning: A portion or unit of something.
examples: Let me give you a piece of advice.
That's a useful piece of information.
Two pieces of evidence were missing.
Hand me a piece of paper.
He cut three pieces of wood to length.
There's one piece of cake left.
She wrote a piece for the local paper.
It's a beautiful piece of music.

senses.head: With abstract uncountables
examples: Let me give you a piece of advice.
That's a useful piece of information.
Two pieces of evidence were missing.

senses.head: With physical materials
examples: Hand me a piece of paper.
He cut three pieces of wood to length.
There's one piece of cake left.

senses.head: A created work
examples: She wrote a piece for the local paper.
It's a beautiful piece of music.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a piece is / two pieces are
entries.contrast: The all-purpose partitive, and the right default for abstract nouns: a piece of advice, information, news, evidence, luck, music, research, work, furniture, equipment, cake, paper. When no more specific word comes to mind, piece is almost never wrong.

entries.meaning: A small amount or portion.
examples: Give me a bit of time.
There's a bit of cheese left.
He needs a bit of luck.
She told me a few bits of news.
I'm a bit tired.
That's a bit much.

senses.head: A small amount
examples: Give me a bit of time.
There's a bit of cheese left.
He needs a bit of luck.
She told me a few bits of news.

senses.head: As an intensifier — a bit
examples: I'm a bit tired.
That's a bit much.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a bit is / two bits are
entries.contrast: A bit of is the informal, smaller-sounding alternative to a piece of: a bit of advice is friendlier than a piece of advice. It also works as an adverb meaning 'slightly' — a bit tired.

entries.meaning: A thin flat piece cut from something.
examples: She toasted two slices of bread.
Add a slice of lemon.
There are three slices of pizza left.
He cut a thin slice of cheese.
Everyone wants a slice of the profits.

senses.head: A cut piece of food
examples: She toasted two slices of bread.
Add a slice of lemon.
There are three slices of pizza left.
He cut a thin slice of cheese.

senses.head: A share or portion
examples: Everyone wants a slice of the profits.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a slice is / two slices are
entries.contrast: Slice means a thin flat piece cut from something larger, so it collocates with bread, cheese, pizza, cake, meat, and lemon — but not with soap or furniture.

entries.meaning: A solid rectangular block of something.
examples: We need another bar of soap.
He ate a whole bar of chocolate.
Two bars of gold were recovered.
The melody enters after four bars.
Iron bars covered the window.

senses.head: A block of a solid substance
examples: We need another bar of soap.
He ate a whole bar of chocolate.
Two bars of gold were recovered.

senses.head: A unit of music
examples: The melody enters after four bars.

senses.head: A long rigid piece of metal
examples: Iron bars covered the window.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a bar is / two bars are
entries.contrast: Bar collocates tightly: a bar of soap, a bar of chocolate, a bar of gold, a bar of music. It does not extend to liquids or powders.

entries.meaning: A thin flat piece of material.
examples: Bring me a sheet of paper.
Two sheets of glass were delivered.
A sheet of ice covered the road.
He cut a sheet of plywood in half.
The sheets need changing.

senses.head: A flat piece of material
examples: Bring me a sheet of paper.
Two sheets of glass were delivered.
A sheet of ice covered the road.
He cut a sheet of plywood in half.

senses.head: Bedding
examples: The sheets need changing.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a sheet is / two sheets are
entries.contrast: A sheet of is used for thin flat materials: paper, glass, metal, ice, plastic. For paper, both a sheet of paper and a piece of paper are normal.

entries.meaning: A set of two matching things, or one object with two joined parts.
examples: Hand me a pair of scissors.
She bought two pairs of jeans.
A pair of glasses was left on the table.
He owns six pairs of shoes.
One pair of socks was missing.
A pair of hawks nests on the roof.

senses.head: With plural-only objects
examples: Hand me a pair of scissors.
She bought two pairs of jeans.
A pair of glasses was left on the table.

senses.head: Two matching items
examples: He owns six pairs of shoes.
One pair of socks was missing.

senses.head: Two people or animals together
examples: A pair of hawks nests on the roof.

entries.agreement: singular when pair is the head — a pair of scissors is missing
entries.contrast: The obligatory partitive for plural-only two-part nouns: a pair of scissors, pants, jeans, glasses, binoculars, pliers. Note the agreement: a pair of scissors is on the desk — the verb follows pair, not scissors.

entries.meaning: A group of things growing or fastened together.
examples: Buy a bunch of bananas.
She brought a bunch of flowers.
Two bunches of grapes were left.
He pulled out a bunch of keys.
A bunch of people are waiting outside.
I have a whole bunch of things to do.

senses.head: Things grouped together
examples: Buy a bunch of bananas.
She brought a bunch of flowers.
Two bunches of grapes were left.
He pulled out a bunch of keys.

senses.head: Informally — a lot of
examples: A bunch of people are waiting outside.
I have a whole bunch of things to do.

entries.agreement: singular as a unit — a bunch of grapes is; plural with people — a bunch of people are
entries.contrast: Bunch collocates with things naturally growing or tied together: grapes, bananas, flowers, keys, herbs. Informally in American English a bunch of also just means 'a lot of', and then takes a plural verb: a bunch of people are waiting.

entries.meaning: A very small amount, held between finger and thumb.
examples: Add a pinch of salt.
Two pinches of saffron is plenty.
Just a pinch of cinnamon on top.
Take what he says with a pinch of salt.
In a pinch, you could use butter instead.

senses.head: A small quantity of a powder
examples: Add a pinch of salt.
Two pinches of saffron is plenty.
Just a pinch of cinnamon on top.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: Take what he says with a pinch of salt.
In a pinch, you could use butter instead.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a pinch is / two pinches are
entries.contrast: Used almost exclusively of dry seasonings: a pinch of salt, a pinch of pepper, a pinch of cinnamon. Literally the amount held between finger and thumb.

entries.meaning: A small round quantity of liquid.
examples: Add two drops of vanilla.
There's not a drop of milk left.
A drop of blood fell on the paper.
Put three drops in each eye.
He hasn't had a drop to drink all evening.

senses.head: A small quantity of liquid
examples: Add two drops of vanilla.
There's not a drop of milk left.
A drop of blood fell on the paper.
Put three drops in each eye.

senses.head: A small amount generally
examples: He hasn't had a drop to drink all evening.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a drop is / two drops are
entries.contrast: The standard partitive for liquids in small quantity: a drop of water, a drop of blood, a drop of oil. For larger amounts use a glass of, a cup of, a bottle of.

entries.meaning: A single small hard particle.
examples: Not a single grain of rice was left.
Grains of sand worked into everything.
A few grains of salt fell on the counter.
There isn't a grain of truth in it.
Cut along the grain, not across it.

senses.head: A single particle
examples: Not a single grain of rice was left.
Grains of sand worked into everything.
A few grains of salt fell on the counter.

senses.head: A tiny amount, figuratively
examples: There isn't a grain of truth in it.

senses.head: The direction of fibers in wood
examples: Cut along the grain, not across it.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a grain is / two grains are
entries.contrast: The partitive for very small hard particles: a grain of rice, a grain of sand, a grain of salt, a grain of truth.

entries.meaning: A compact shapeless mass.
examples: Two lumps of sugar, please.
He threw a lump of coal on the fire.
She rolled the lump of dough flat.
The doctor found a small lump.
I got a lump in my throat just watching it.

senses.head: A shapeless mass
examples: Two lumps of sugar, please.
He threw a lump of coal on the fire.
She rolled the lump of dough flat.

senses.head: A swelling on the body
examples: The doctor found a small lump.

senses.head: In fixed expressions
examples: I got a lump in my throat just watching it.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a lump is / two lumps are
entries.contrast: Used of shapeless solid masses: a lump of sugar, a lump of coal, a lump of clay, a lump of dough. Compare bar, which implies a regular rectangular shape.

entries.meaning: The container, and the amount it holds.
examples: We opened a bottle of wine.
Buy two bottles of olive oil.
He drank a whole bottle of water.
Put the empty bottles in the recycling.
The bottle is made of thick green glass.

senses.head: The amount a bottle holds
examples: We opened a bottle of wine.
Buy two bottles of olive oil.
He drank a whole bottle of water.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: Put the empty bottles in the recycling.
The bottle is made of thick green glass.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a bottle is / two bottles are
entries.contrast: Container partitives are the easiest group, because the container is visible: a bottle of wine, a can of soup, a jar of honey, a carton of milk, a bag of flour, a box of cereal, a tube of toothpaste.

entries.meaning: The metal container, and the amount it holds.
examples: Add a can of crushed tomatoes.
We bought three cans of soup.
He drank a can of soda.
The empty cans go in the blue bin.
Open the can carefully — the edge is sharp.

senses.head: The amount a can holds
examples: Add a can of crushed tomatoes.
We bought three cans of soup.
He drank a can of soda.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: The empty cans go in the blue bin.
Open the can carefully — the edge is sharp.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a can is / two cans are
entries.variants: the British word for the food container is tin
entries.contrast: American can, British tin, for the same sealed metal container. Both languages say a can of soda.

entries.meaning: The wide-mouthed container, and the amount it holds.
examples: There's half a jar of jam left.
Two jars of honey came from one hive.
She opened a jar of pickles.
The jars are sterilized before filling.
He keeps screws in an old jar.

senses.head: The amount a jar holds
examples: There's half a jar of jam left.
Two jars of honey came from one hive.
She opened a jar of pickles.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: The jars are sterilized before filling.
He keeps screws in an old jar.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a jar is / two jars are
entries.contrast: A jar is wide-mouthed, usually glass, and holds thick or solid food: a jar of honey, a jar of jam, a jar of pickles. A bottle is narrow-necked and holds liquid.

entries.meaning: The cardboard container, and the amount it holds.
examples: Pick up a carton of milk.
Two cartons of eggs should be enough.
He drank half a carton of juice.
Flatten the cartons before recycling.
The carton was leaking at the bottom.

senses.head: The amount a carton holds
examples: Pick up a carton of milk.
Two cartons of eggs should be enough.
He drank half a carton of juice.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: Flatten the cartons before recycling.
The carton was leaking at the bottom.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a carton is / two cartons are
entries.contrast: In American English a carton of milk and a carton of eggs are both standard, though the containers are quite different. For juice, a carton is the paper container and a bottle the plastic one.

entries.meaning: A wrapped package, and the amount it holds.
examples: Buy a pack of batteries.
Two packs of gum were in his pocket.
She opened a fresh pack of cards.
A pack of wolves crossed the ridge.
He shouldered his pack and started walking.

senses.head: A wrapped quantity
examples: Buy a pack of batteries.
Two packs of gum were in his pocket.
She opened a fresh pack of cards.

senses.head: A group of animals
examples: A pack of wolves crossed the ridge.

senses.head: A backpack
examples: He shouldered his pack and started walking.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a pack is / two packs are
entries.variants: packet is the usual British word for a small pack
entries.contrast: Also a collective noun for animals — a pack of wolves, a pack of dogs — and a group of playing cards.

entries.meaning: A shaped mass of bread.
examples: Pick up a loaf of bread.
Two loaves were still warm.
She bakes a loaf every Sunday.
Half a loaf is better than none.
He cut the loaf into thick slices.

senses.head: A whole bread
examples: Pick up a loaf of bread.
Two loaves were still warm.
She bakes a loaf every Sunday.
Half a loaf is better than none.
He cut the loaf into thick slices.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a loaf is / two loaves are
entries.contrast: The obligatory partitive for bread, which is uncountable: ✗ two breads is wrong, two loaves of bread is right. Note the irregular plural loaves — see loaf.

entries.meaning: The drinking vessel, and the amount it holds; in cooking, a fixed measure.
examples: She made a cup of tea.
Two cups of coffee is my limit.
He drank three cups of water.
Add two cups of flour.
The recipe calls for a cup of sugar.
They lifted the cup for the third year running.

senses.head: A drink's worth
examples: She made a cup of tea.
Two cups of coffee is my limit.
He drank three cups of water.

senses.head: A cooking measure
examples: Add two cups of flour.
The recipe calls for a cup of sugar.

senses.head: A trophy
examples: They lifted the cup for the third year running.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a cup is / two cups are
entries.contrast: In American recipes a cup is a fixed measure — eight fluid ounces — not just a drinking vessel. This is why American recipes measure flour and sugar by volume where European ones use weight.

entries.meaning: The round deep dish, and the amount it holds.
examples: He ate two bowls of cereal.
A bowl of soup comes with the sandwich.
She had a bowl of rice and nothing else.
All the bowls are in the dishwasher.
He dropped a bowl on the tile floor.

senses.head: The amount a bowl holds
examples: He ate two bowls of cereal.
A bowl of soup comes with the sandwich.
She had a bowl of rice and nothing else.

senses.head: The dish itself
examples: All the bowls are in the dishwasher.
He dropped a bowl on the tile floor.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a bowl is / two bowls are
entries.contrast: Collocates with soup, cereal, rice, and soup-like foods: a bowl of soup, a bowl of cereal. Not used for solids you would slice.

entries.meaning: The flat dish, and the amount it holds.
examples: She brought out a plate of cookies.
Two plates of pasta arrived at once.
He filled his plate twice.
All the plates match except one.
Stack the plates by the sink.

senses.head: The amount a plate holds
examples: She brought out a plate of cookies.
Two plates of pasta arrived at once.
He filled his plate twice.

senses.head: The dish itself
examples: All the plates match except one.
Stack the plates by the sink.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a plate is / two plates are
entries.contrast: A plate of implies a flat serving: a plate of pasta, a plate of cookies. Liquids take a bowl or a cup.

entries.meaning: The flexible container, and the amount it holds.
examples: Buy a bag of flour.
Two bags of ice should be enough.
He carried three bags of groceries.
A bag of chips costs almost nothing.
She left her bag on the train.

senses.head: The amount a bag holds
examples: Buy a bag of flour.
Two bags of ice should be enough.
He carried three bags of groceries.
A bag of chips costs almost nothing.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: She left her bag on the train.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a bag is / two bags are
entries.contrast: The default container partitive for loose dry goods: a bag of flour, a bag of rice, a bag of chips, a bag of groceries.

entries.meaning: The rigid container, and the amount it holds.
examples: Buy a box of cereal.
Two boxes of tissues went in a week.
He gave her a box of chocolates.
All the boxes are still in the garage.
Break the boxes down before recycling.

senses.head: The amount a box holds
examples: Buy a box of cereal.
Two boxes of tissues went in a week.
He gave her a box of chocolates.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: All the boxes are still in the garage.
Break the boxes down before recycling.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a box is / two boxes are
entries.contrast: Note the plural takes -es because of the final x: boxes, not ✗ boxs. Collocates with cereal, tissues, matches, chocolates.

entries.meaning: The cylindrical squeeze container, and the amount it holds.
examples: We need a new tube of toothpaste.
Two tubes of glue were used up.
She squeezed the last of the tube onto the brush.
A tube of oil paint lasts a long time.
Both tubes had split at the seam.

senses.head: The amount a tube holds
examples: We need a new tube of toothpaste.
Two tubes of glue were used up.
She squeezed the last of the tube onto the brush.
A tube of oil paint lasts a long time.

senses.head: The container itself
examples: Both tubes had split at the seam.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a tube is / two tubes are
entries.contrast: The obligatory partitive for paste products: a tube of toothpaste, a tube of glue, a tube of paint. ✗ A bottle of toothpaste is wrong.

entries.meaning: The wound cylinder, and the amount it holds.
examples: Buy two rolls of paper towels.
A roll of tape costs a dollar.
He used up an entire roll of film.
Three rolls of quarters were in the drawer.
The soup comes with a roll.

senses.head: The amount a roll holds
examples: Buy two rolls of paper towels.
A roll of tape costs a dollar.
He used up an entire roll of film.
Three rolls of quarters were in the drawer.

senses.head: A small round loaf
examples: The soup comes with a roll.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a roll is / two rolls are
entries.contrast: For anything wound around a core: a roll of paper towels, a roll of tape, a roll of film, a roll of coins.

entries.meaning: The elongated piece, and the amount it holds.
examples: Add one stick of butter.
Two sticks of gum were left in the pack.
She chopped three sticks of celery.
A stick of butter is half a cup.
He threw a stick for the dog.

senses.head: A measured piece
examples: Add one stick of butter.
Two sticks of gum were left in the pack.
She chopped three sticks of celery.
A stick of butter is half a cup.

senses.head: A thin piece of wood
examples: He threw a stick for the dog.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a stick is / two sticks are
entries.contrast: In American cooking a stick of butter is a standard unit — half a cup, four ounces — and recipes assume it. Also a stick of gum, a stick of celery.

entries.meaning: One segment of a garlic bulb; also the spice.
examples: Crush two cloves of garlic.
A single clove is plenty for this.
The recipe calls for six cloves.
Add a few whole cloves to the pot.
Clove is the dominant flavor here.

senses.head: A garlic segment
examples: Crush two cloves of garlic.
A single clove is plenty for this.
The recipe calls for six cloves.

senses.head: The spice
examples: Add a few whole cloves to the pot.
Clove is the dominant flavor here.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a clove is / two cloves are
entries.contrast: A clove of garlic is one segment; the whole thing is a head or a bulb of garlic. Confusingly, cloves is also an unrelated spice.

entries.meaning: The compact rounded mass of a vegetable.
examples: Buy a head of lettuce.
Two heads of garlic will last a month.
She chopped a whole head of cabbage.
Both heads of broccoli had gone yellow.
A head of cauliflower feeds four.

senses.head: A rounded vegetable
examples: Buy a head of lettuce.
Two heads of garlic will last a month.
She chopped a whole head of cabbage.
Both heads of broccoli had gone yellow.
A head of cauliflower feeds four.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a head is / two heads are
entries.contrast: As a food partitive, head takes a regular plural: two heads of lettuce. That is different from the livestock-counting sense, where it stays unchanged: fifty head of cattle.

entries.meaning: A very small quantity added to something.
examples: Add a dash of hot sauce.
Two dashes of bitters go in the glass.
She takes her coffee with a dash of cream.
A dash of salt brings out the sweetness.
The speech had a dash of real feeling in it.

senses.head: A small quantity
examples: Add a dash of hot sauce.
Two dashes of bitters go in the glass.
She takes her coffee with a dash of cream.
A dash of salt brings out the sweetness.

senses.head: A small amount of a quality
examples: The speech had a dash of real feeling in it.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a dash is / two dashes are
entries.contrast: Smaller and more casual than a measured amount, and used mainly of liquids and strong seasonings: a dash of salt, a dash of bitters, a dash of milk.

entries.meaning: A small quantity of liquid poured in.
examples: Add a splash of white wine to the pan.
Just a splash of milk, thanks.
Two splashes of vinegar finish the sauce.
She poured a splash of oil into the skillet.
A splash of soda water lightens it.

senses.head: A small quantity of liquid
examples: Add a splash of white wine to the pan.
Just a splash of milk, thanks.
Two splashes of vinegar finish the sauce.
She poured a splash of oil into the skillet.
A splash of soda water lightens it.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a splash is / two splashes are
entries.contrast: Used only of liquids, and slightly larger than a dash: a splash of wine, a splash of milk.

entries.meaning: A heap of things.
examples: There's a pile of laundry on the bed.
Two piles of books blocked the door.
He has a pile of work to get through.
She sorted everything into three piles.
They made a pile of money on that deal.

senses.head: A heap
examples: There's a pile of laundry on the bed.
Two piles of books blocked the door.
He has a pile of work to get through.
She sorted everything into three piles.

senses.head: A large amount
examples: They made a pile of money on that deal.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a pile is / two piles are
entries.contrast: A pile of is informal and works with almost anything, countable or not — a pile of laundry, a pile of books, a pile of work. Compare a stack, which implies neat ordering.

entries.meaning: A neat ordered heap.
examples: A stack of plates sat by the sink.
Two stacks of paper filled the tray.
He carried a stack of books to the counter.
She ordered a stack of pancakes.
Both stacks were exactly the same height.

senses.head: An ordered heap
examples: A stack of plates sat by the sink.
Two stacks of paper filled the tray.
He carried a stack of books to the counter.
She ordered a stack of pancakes.
Both stacks were exactly the same height.

entries.agreement: follows the partitive — a stack is / two stacks are
entries.contrast: A stack is neatly ordered; a pile is not. A stack of plates is stable; a pile of plates sounds precarious.
